_README.purpose: Per-country licensing and seasonal guidance. ONE source of truth, keyed by the ISO code in src/lib/countries.ts. Read by src/pages/CountryHub.tsx, src/pages/Regulations.tsx and scripts/prerender.mjs. It replaced src/data/regulation-regions.json, which held a second copy of the same licensing facts for /regulations only — two copies of a licence rule drift, and a stale licence claim is the kind of error a reader can be fined for following.
_README.rules: CLAUDE.md content rules apply in full. Every factual claim here traces to a government fisheries agency, a statutory licensing body or a national park authority — the URLs in `authority` and `links` are those sources. Guide sites, blogs and forums are NOT sources (see the Islamorada lesson in CLAUDE.md). No bag limits and no size limits anywhere in this file, ever: they change constantly, go stale silently, and rule 3 forbids them. Fees and prices are also left out — they date faster than anything else.
_README.fields: authority = primary official licensing body. links = further official pages. regulations = 2-4 sentences for /regulations. licensing / seasons / water = the hub paragraphs. sourcing = 'full' where every claim in the prose was verified against an official page this session, 'partial' where something in the country's existing blurb could not be verified and was therefore left out. sourceNotes records exactly what is unverified so the next person does not have to rediscover it. sourcing and sourceNotes are metadata and are never rendered.
_README.seasons: The seasonal paragraphs describe the fishing seasons of the spots AnglerDeck already publishes, drawn from the researched `best_times` and `regulations` on those spot rows. Statutory closed seasons are stated only where an official source confirms them.

links.name: NSW recreational fishing fee — exemptions
NT Government — about recreational fishing

AU.regulations: Australia licenses fishing state by state, and the rules change as you cross a border. New South Wales requires the Recreational Fishing Fee for both fresh and salt water, and you must carry the receipt while fishing. The Northern Territory requires no recreational fishing licence at all. Confirm with the agency for the state you are fishing before you travel, because none of them defers to the others.
AU.licensing: There is no Australian fishing licence. Each state and territory runs its own system, and the difference between neighbours is large enough to catch visitors out. New South Wales requires the Recreational Fishing Fee for both fresh and salt water, sold in short-term and multi-year forms, and you must carry proof of payment while you fish; the state publishes a list of exemptions, including anglers fishing under a guide or charter operator who holds an exemption certificate. The Northern Territory is the opposite case and requires no recreational licence whatsoever, though boating rules, closed areas and Aboriginal land permissions all still apply. Because the border matters more than the country, check the state agency rather than any national page — and on the Murray, check which bank you are standing on.
AU.seasons: Australia's fishing year runs on the tropical wet and the southern temperate seasons at once, and the two are almost opposites. In the north, the barramundi fishing we cover keys off the monsoon: the run-off after the wet, roughly February to April, and the build-up from October to December. Cairns marlin fishing is a defined heavy-tackle season from September to December, while the reef itself fishes year-round. In the south the pattern is conventional — Sydney kingfish from spring through autumn, Murray cod best in summer and settling into autumn. Murray cod also carry a statutory closure: the stretch from Yarrawonga Weir to the Tocumwal Road Bridge is closed to all fishing from 1 September to 30 November, not merely closed to cod.
AU.water: The Australian spots on AnglerDeck are mostly saltwater, and they span nearly the whole continent. Darwin Harbour is tidal creek and mangrove country for barramundi, threadfin salmon, mangrove jack and queenfish, fished around making tides at the creek mouths. Cairns sits on the black marlin grounds outside the Great Barrier Reef, with Spanish mackerel, coral trout and yellowfin tuna on the same trip. Sydney Harbour is genuinely urban saltwater for yellowtail kingfish, bream, flathead and tailor. Inland, the Murray at Yarrawonga is the country's iconic native freshwater fishery, for Murray cod and golden perch in slow, timbered water. Hervey Bay adds shallow flats and winter whiting. Difficulty runs from beginner to advanced, so there is something here for a first trip and something for a serious one.
AU.sourceNotes: NSW fee and NT no-licence position verified against dpi.nsw.gov.au and nt.gov.au. Queensland's no-general-licence position for tidal waters, and the Victorian and Tasmanian licence requirements asserted in the countries.ts blurb, were NOT verified this session — no claim about them is made in this prose. The Yarrawonga all-fishing closure and the Cairns season come from the existing researched spot rows, not from a fresh agency fetch. SOUTH AUSTRALIA, attempted 7 Sep 2026 for the /guides article and NOT verified: the countries.ts blurb claims South Australia requires no general recreational licence. Every South Australian government host refused the fetcher outright — pir.sa.gov.au (and www.), sa.gov.au, sawater.com.au, reservoirs.sa.gov.au and legislation.sa.gov.au all returned HTTP 403, and web.archive.org is unavailable to it. This is fetcher-blocked, not source-blocked: PIRSA does publish recreational fishing rules, so a real browser should settle it in one visit (pir.sa.gov.au/fishing-and-aquaculture/recreational-fishing/rules). Search summaries assert the no-licence position and that reservoir fishing needs a SA Water permit, but a search summary is not a source, so nothing about South Australia is stated in this prose or in the /guides article. Confirm the reservoir permit exception at the same time — a bare 'no licence in SA' would be incomplete without it.

authority.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — purchase a fishing license

links.name: NOAA Fisheries — recreational fishing resources

US.regulations: State fish and wildlife agencies, not the federal government, license fishing in the United States, and every state sets its own rules. You need a licence from the state where you fish; most sell online, by phone or through retail agents. State waters generally run from the shore out to three nautical miles, and federal waters beyond that are managed by NOAA Fisheries. Look up the state, not the country.
US.licensing: Fishing licences in the United States are issued by state fish and wildlife agencies, and the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service is explicit that you need a licence from the state where the fishing happens and must meet that state's conditions. Most states sell online, by phone or through tackle shops and other retail agents, and most offer short-term non-resident options that suit a trip. Saltwater is where visitors most often go wrong: several states require a separate saltwater licence or enrolment in a marine registry on top of the freshwater one, and some species carry their own stamp or tag. Jurisdiction changes offshore too — state waters typically extend three nautical miles, and federal waters beyond that fall to NOAA Fisheries. Budget time for this before the trip rather than at the ramp.
US.seasons: The United States is wide enough that its fishing seasons barely overlap, and the spots we cover show it. Florida Keys tarpon are a spring and early-summer migration, roughly April to July, worked on moving tides. Alaska's Kenai runs to the salmon calendar instead: a first sockeye run in June, a heavier second run through July and August, then big rainbows in September and October as the salmon spawn. Montana's Madison is a hatch-driven trout river, with the salmonfly coming off in late June and July, caddis in the evenings and a brown trout run in autumn — and in hot summers the state can impose 'hoot owl' restrictions that close fishing in the afternoons. Louisiana's marsh peaks with the autumn bull redfish run from September to November.
US.water: The four published US spots are deliberately different from one another. Islamorada is Florida Keys flats fishing for tarpon, bonefish, permit and snook — shallow, sight-fished and technical. The Kenai is big, cold, glacial-fed water in Alaska for king and sockeye salmon and the rainbow trout that follow them. The Madison at Ennis is classic Rocky Mountain fly water for brown and rainbow trout. Venice, Louisiana is marsh and delta fishing for redfish and speckled trout, with yellowfin tuna reachable offshore from the same port — and it is the beginner-friendly one of the four. Between them they cover saltwater flats, salmon rivers, a trout river and a delta, which is a reasonable sample of what American fishing actually is.
US.sourceNotes: The federal position — state agencies license fishing, state waters to three nautical miles, NOAA beyond — verified against fws.gov and fisheries.noaa.gov. Individual state requirements (Florida non-resident saltwater, Alaska king salmon stamp, Montana conservation licence, Louisiana basic-plus-saltwater) come from the existing researched spot rows and were NOT re-verified against each state agency this session, so the prose describes the pattern rather than naming any state's specific licence.

authority.name: Fisheries and Oceans Canada — recreational fishing licences (Pacific)

links.name: DFO — salmon conservation stamps

CA.regulations: Canada splits licensing between two levels of government. Freshwater licences are provincial, so the province sets the rules for lakes and rivers. Tidal water is federal: everyone fishing in British Columbia's salt water needs a DFO Tidal Waters Sport Fishing licence, available for one, three or five days or annually. Keeping Pacific salmon additionally requires a Salmon Conservation Stamp, which is not needed if you release everything.
CA.licensing: Canada is the country where visitors most often buy the wrong licence, because two governments are involved. Freshwater fishing is provincial, so an Alberta or New Brunswick licence comes from that province and covers only it. Tidal water in British Columbia is federal: Fisheries and Oceans Canada requires every recreational angler to hold a Tidal Waters Sport Fishing licence, sold as one-, three- and five-day or annual, and available online through the National Recreational Licensing System or from retail outlets, charters, lodges and marinas acting as access providers. If you intend to keep Pacific salmon you also need a Salmon Conservation Stamp affixed to that licence — it runs from 1 April to 31 March and is not required if you release every salmon you catch. Atlantic salmon in the east is licensed separately again by the province.
CA.seasons: Canadian seasons are short, sharp and worth planning a trip around. On the Miramichi, Atlantic salmon come in two waves — a summer run in June and July and an autumn run in September and October — and both respond to rain lifting the water. British Columbia's Campbell River fishes chinook from July to September and coho in September and October, worked around the tide changes. Alberta's Bow River is a year-round trout river with a strong summer terrestrial season: hopper fishing from July into September, blue-winged olive hatches, then streamer fishing in autumn. In-season change is normal rather than exceptional on the coast, where DFO adjusts area closures and retention through the season, so check current notices rather than last year's plan.
CA.water: Three published Canadian spots, three different fisheries. The Miramichi in New Brunswick is one of the great Atlantic salmon rivers, fished for salmon and brook trout, and largely a live-release fishery. The Bow, running straight through Calgary, is an unusually accessible brown and rainbow trout river — a tailwater with city access and serious fish. Campbell River on Vancouver Island is Pacific saltwater for chinook and coho salmon and halibut, fished from boats around the tides. The mix means the licence you need depends entirely on which one you pick: provincial for the first two, federal plus a stamp for the third.
CA.sourceNotes: BC tidal licence, licence durations, access providers and the Salmon Conservation Stamp (including that it is unnecessary for release-only fishing, and its 1 April to 31 March validity) verified against pac.dfo-mpo.gc.ca. Provincial freshwater licensing stated only in general terms.

authority.name: Fish & Game New Zealand — licences and regulations

links.name: DOC — buy a Taupō fishing licence
DOC — Lake Rotoaira licences

NZ.regulations: New Zealand requires no licence for recreational sea fishing, but freshwater is licensed. A Fish & Game licence covers the whole country with one important exception: the Taupō Fishing District is administered by the Department of Conservation and needs its own separate licence, and Lake Rotoaira is a separate district again with its own. Bag and size limits apply in the sea — check Fisheries New Zealand before keeping anything.
NZ.licensing: Sea fishing in New Zealand needs no licence, which makes the freshwater rules the only paperwork most visitors face — and there is one trap in them. Fish & Game New Zealand licences cover the entire country apart from the Taupō area, which the Department of Conservation administers instead. A Fish & Game licence is not valid in the Taupō Fishing District; you need a DOC Taupō licence, bought separately. Lake Rotoaira is a further separate district with its own licences and regulations again. Since two of the three New Zealand spots we publish sit inside the Taupō district, this is the single most useful thing to know before travelling here. Biosecurity rules also bite: felt-soled wading boots are banned nationwide, and gear should be cleaned between waterways.
NZ.seasons: New Zealand's trout fishing is a winter story, which surprises northern-hemisphere visitors. The Tongariro's rainbow run climbs from June to September, best after fresh rain, and Lake Taupō follows the same spawning-run calendar from May to September, with evening smelting at the river mouths and deep trolling through summer. Saltwater inverts it: the Bay of Islands game season runs January to May over the southern summer, while snapper are available year-round and the fishing keys off tide changes around the islands. So a June trip and a February trip to New Zealand are two entirely different holidays, and it is worth deciding which one you are taking before you book.
NZ.water: The New Zealand spots split cleanly between the Taupō trout fishery and the northern game coast. The Tongariro at Tūrangi is the country's most famous run river, for rainbow and brown trout, mostly fly water. Lake Taupō itself is the beginner-friendly counterpart — the same fish in a very large lake, fished from boat and shore. The Bay of Islands in Northland is the opposite discipline: advanced offshore fishing for striped marlin and yellowtail kingfish, with snapper as the everyday species. Two licences, one of which does not exist anywhere else in the country, and one fishery that needs none at all.
NZ.sourceNotes: Fish & Game national coverage, the Taupō district exception under DOC, and Lake Rotoaira as a separate district all verified against fishandgame.org.nz and doc.govt.nz. Sea fishing needing no licence is stated in general terms; specific bag and size limits deliberately omitted under rule 3.

GB.regulations: You must hold a rod fishing licence for England and Wales to fish for salmon, trout, freshwater fish, smelt or eel with rod and line — including on private lakes and club waters, where you also need the owner's permission. Children under 13 do not need one, and 13-to-16 licences are free. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different rules entirely; the River Tweed is outside the England and Wales licence. Sea angling needs no licence.
GB.licensing: The United Kingdom is really two systems. In England and Wales you must hold an Environment Agency rod licence to fish for salmon, trout, freshwater fish, smelt or eel with a rod and line, and GOV.UK is explicit that this applies on private water too — angling club lakes and private fisheries included. The licence is permission to hold a rod, not permission to fish a particular water, so you still need the owner's or fishery's consent. Children under 13 do not need a licence and 13-to-16-year-olds hold a free junior one. Scotland issues no rod licence at all; instead you need a permit from whoever owns the beat, usually an estate or a District Salmon Fishery Board. The Tweed is administered separately from the England and Wales licence, and Northern Ireland is different again. Sea angling is free throughout.
GB.seasons: British game fishing is strongly seasonal and traditional about it. The Spey fishes a spring run in April and May and summer grilse from June to August, with rising water after rain the thing to wait for. The Tweed is the autumn river — a September-to-November run that is among the best-known in Europe — with spring fish from February to April. Hampshire's Test is a chalkstream on a different calendar again: mayfly in late May and June, an evening rise through summer, and grayling into autumn and winter. Two Scottish rules shape any trip: there is no salmon fishing on Sundays, and mandatory catch-and-release applies early in the season.
GB.water: All three published UK spots are advanced fly water, which is a fair reflection of what Britain is known for rather than all it offers. The Spey in Speyside and the Tweed in the Borders are Atlantic salmon and sea trout rivers, fished from estate beats, with the Tweed also holding grayling. The Test at Stockbridge is the archetypal southern English chalkstream for brown trout and grayling — clear, weedy, spring-fed water where many beats are dry-fly-only and upstream-only. On all three, access is the real constraint rather than the licence: nearly every beat is private, so a day ticket, a syndicate rod or an estate booking is what actually gets you fishing.
GB.sourceNotes: Species covered, application to private water, the under-13 exemption, free 13-16 junior licence, exclusion of the Tweed, and the different rules in Scotland and Northern Ireland all verified verbatim against gov.uk/fishing-licences. Scottish beat-permit practice and the Sunday rule come from the existing researched spot rows.

links.name: LALLF M-V — fishing documents overview
LALLF M-V — Fischereischein examination

DE.regulations: Germany licenses fishing at state level, and in most states a Fischereischein follows an examination — which makes casual visiting genuinely difficult. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is the exception and issues a Touristenfischereischein with no exam, valid in its coastal and inland waters for up to 28 consecutive days and renewable within the calendar year. A separate permit for the specific water is required on top of the licence everywhere. Check the state authority before you travel.
DE.licensing: Germany is the hardest country on this list to fish on impulse, and it is worth understanding why before booking. Fishing law is made by each federal state, and the standard route to a Fischereischein is passing a state fishing examination covering fish species, tackle, law and animal welfare — not something a visitor arranges in a fortnight. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern deliberately built an exception: its state authority issues a Touristenfischereischein to people who do not hold an exam-based licence, valid in the state's coastal and inland waters for up to 28 consecutive days, extendable more than once in the same calendar year, and available from local authorities and issuing offices or digitally since December 2024. No exam is required; instead you receive an information brochure and are obliged to learn from it. In every German state, the licence is only half of it — you also need an Erlaubnisschein for the particular water.
DE.seasons: German fishing runs on a temperate calendar with real closed seasons behind it. On the Müritz lakes, autumn is the pike window from September to November, zander fish best at dusk, and spring fishing opens up after the closed season ends. The Rhine at Karlsruhe is a summer-nights and autumn-feeding river, and it responds to a rise in water. Pike and zander both carry closed seasons and minimum sizes, and because the dates are set by each state rather than nationally, the same species can be open on one side of a state boundary and closed on the other. Night fishing rules and permitted baits vary the same way, so read the rules for the specific water.
DE.water: Both published German spots are freshwater, and they are opposites in character. The Müritz lakes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern are a large, shallow, connected lake district — beginner-friendly water for northern pike, zander and perch, and the one part of Germany a visitor can realistically fish without an exam. The Rhine at Karlsruhe is big-river fishing in Baden-Württemberg: powerful, industrialised water holding carp, pike and wels catfish, and an intermediate proposition at best because reading current and finding fish matters more than casting. If you are coming to Germany specifically to fish, the licensing rules alone argue for Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
DE.sourceNotes: The Touristenfischereischein — no exam, up to 28 consecutive days, multiple extensions per calendar year, issued by local authorities or digitally since 10 December 2024, brochure obligation — verified against lallf.de, the M-V state authority. That the standard Fischereischein follows a state examination is verified by the same source's framing and its separate examination page. Fee amounts deliberately omitted. State-by-state closed-season dates are not enumerated because they are set per Land.

authority.name: Fédération Nationale de la Pêche en France — cartedepeche.fr

links.name: Ministère de la Mer — pêche de loisir en mer
Légifrance — Code rural et de la pêche maritime, pêche maritime de loisir (R921-83 à R921-93)
Légifrance — arrêté du 7 novembre 2025, conditions d'exercice de la pêche de loisir en mer

FR.regulations: Freshwater fishing in France requires a carte de pêche, which is membership of a local AAPPMA — an approved fishing and aquatic environment protection association — sold through the national federation's site as daily, weekly or annual cards, with reduced options for under-18s and a discovery card for children. An interfederal card extends coverage across participating départements. Closed seasons for pike and zander are set at département level, so check locally. Recreational sea fishing sits outside the carte de pêche under the maritime fishing code, but it is not paperwork-free: since early 2026 sea anglers aged 16 and over who target the species listed by ministerial order must register and declare those catches the same day.
FR.licensing: To fish fresh water in France you need a carte de pêche, and the card is really an association membership: it enrols you in an AAPPMA, one of the approved local fishing and aquatic-environment protection associations, within the national recreational fishing network. The Fédération Nationale de la Pêche en France sells them centrally, which makes this one of the easier systems in Europe for a visitor — you can buy a daily card, a weekly card or an annual one, and there are reduced categories for minors, a discovery card for under-12s and a women's discovery card. Anglers wanting more than one département should look at the interfederal annual card. Sea angling is governed separately from the carte de pêche, and the rules there changed in 2026. The maritime fishing code subjects recreational sea fishing to the same provisions as professional fishing on minimum sizes, permitted gear, fishing zones and periods, and allows specific recreational activities to be made subject to authorisation by ministerial order. One such order now applies broadly: recreational sea anglers aged 16 and over targeting the species it lists must register — a registration valid twelve months, made through the European Commission's recreational fisheries platform or the RecFishing app — and must declare catches of those species on the day they are taken. So sea angling in France is outside the carte de pêche system, but it is no longer outside the paperwork. Closed seasons for pike and zander are set départementally, so the rules that matter are the local ones.
FR.seasons: France offers two quite different seasons depending on whether you face the Atlantic or inland. On the Brittany coast, European bass fishing runs from May to October, and the useful detail is tidal rather than monthly — the two hours either side of low water, at dawn and dusk. Inland on the Loire, summer nights are for wels catfish, autumn is the zander window, and spring pike fishing opens once the closed season ends. That closed season is the thing to plan around: the dates are set by the département, so a pike trip booked on national information can arrive to find the water shut. The Brittany bass season and the Loire predator season overlap enough that a summer trip can reasonably do both.
FR.water: The two published French spots deliberately cover both sides of French fishing. The Brittany bass coast in Finistère is rock, reef and beach saltwater fishing for European bass, pollack and mackerel, worked on the tide — no licence needed, so it is the more spontaneous of the two. The Loire at Tours is big, slow, warm river water for wels catfish, zander and northern pike, and the catfish there grow to a size that surprises people who think of the Loire as a scenic river rather than a predator fishery. Both are intermediate: neither needs specialist skills, both reward knowing when to be there.
FR.sourceNotes: The carte de pêche requirement, AAPPMA membership model, FNPF as operator, and the daily/weekly/annual and minor/discovery card range all verified against cartedepeche.fr. STILL NOT VERIFIED, and still deliberately absent: that recreational SEA fishing requires no licence in France, which the countries.ts blurb and the existing spot row both assert. Re-attempted 7 Sep 2026 for the /guides article. cartedepeche.fr does not address sea fishing; mer.gouv.fr's pêche-de-loisir-en-mer page covers only the new registration duty and never states the licence position; the mesdemarches.agriculture.gouv.fr page 301s to a URL that 404s; the mer.gouv.fr flyer is a binary PDF; and no service-public.fr fiche states it either. What the code does say (R921-84, R921-85, verified on Légifrance) is that recreational sea fishing is subject to the professional provisions on sizes, gear, zones and periods, and that authorisation regimes MAY be imposed on activities listed by ministerial order — which makes licence-free an inference from an enabling provision, not a stated rule, so it stays out. NEWLY VERIFIED and now in the prose: the arrêté du 7 novembre 2025 (Légifrance) requires recreational sea anglers aged 16+ targeting the annexed species to register for twelve months via the European Commission recreational fisheries platform or the RecFishing app, and to declare those catches the same day. Two discrepancies between official sources are the reason the prose says only 'since early 2026' and names no species: the arrêté says registration applies from 10 January 2026 while mer.gouv.fr says 12 February 2026, and their species lists differ (the arrêté's annexe includes bluefin tuna where the ministry page lists mackerel). Lead for the IT entry, not acted on: RecFishing is a European Commission app, so Italy's RecFishing claim may be confirmable from an EU source — but an Italian official page is still what that entry needs.

links.name: MAPA — PescaREC catch reporting

ES.regulations: Spain issues recreational fishing licences through its autonomous communities, not nationally — so the licence you need depends on the region. For sea fishing, the national ministry additionally requires anglers holding a regional recreational maritime licence to register and report their catches daily through the PescaREC app, whether fishing from shore, a vessel, a floating device or underwater. Inland licences are regional too, and conditions differ between communities.
ES.licensing: Spanish licensing is regional: each autonomous community issues its own recreational fishing licences, and one region's licence does not cover another. That applies inland and at sea, and the ministry's own description of recreational sea fishing assumes you hold a recreational maritime licence issued by an autonomous community or autonomous city. On top of the regional licence, Spain now layers a national reporting duty at sea: the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food runs PescaREC, an app through which recreational sea anglers register and report their catches daily, and through which specific authorisation is requested for species under differentiated protection measures. It applies from shore as well as from a boat. Practically, that means a Spanish sea trip involves two steps — the regional licence first, then daily reporting — and guides and lodges commonly arrange the first for visiting anglers.
ES.seasons: The two Spanish spots we publish run on different clocks. The Strait of Gibraltar has a bluefin tuna run from April to July, and the limiting factor there is not the calendar but the levante wind — the fishing happens between wind spells, on slack current. The Ebro at Mequinenza is a warm-water predator fishery: summer nights for wels catfish, a spring pre-spawn window from April to June, and an autumn feeding period. Bluefin is quota-managed and requires specific authorisation, which in practice makes it a largely catch-and-release fishery for recreational anglers — one of the clearest cases on the site where the paperwork, not the season, determines what the day looks like.
ES.water: Spain gives AnglerDeck one of its most extreme saltwater spots and one of its best-known freshwater ones. Tarifa, on the Strait of Gibraltar, is advanced big-game water where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, for bluefin tuna, albacore and amberjack in strong current. The Ebro at Mequinenza in Aragón is the opposite: a deep, slow reservoir stretch that has become one of Europe's most famous wels catfish and carp fisheries, also holding zander. It is intermediate water where guides and lodges do much of the work, and it is the reason a great many anglers visit Spain at all.
ES.sourceNotes: PescaREC — ministry app, daily catch reporting, applies from land/vessel/underwater/floating devices, presupposes a regional recreational maritime licence, and handles authorisation for specially protected species — verified against mapa.gob.es. Regional issuance of licences verified from the same source. NOT verified: that inland licences in some communities require an examination in Spanish (claimed in the countries.ts blurb), that the sea licence is usually free, and the March 2026 PescaREC start date in the existing spot row — none of these are stated in this prose.

links.name: MASAF — notification of recreational sea fishing activity

IT.regulations: Italy runs two systems. Recreational sea fishing requires a notification (comunicazione) to the national agriculture ministry, MASAF, through its sport-fishing census — a process whose online access uses Italian digital identity credentials (SPID, CIE or CNS). Freshwater licences are issued regionally instead, and many waters need a further daily or seasonal permit from the local association. Rod numbers, trolling rules and closed seasons all vary by region.
IT.licensing: Italian sea fishing is free of charge but not free of paperwork: MASAF, the national agriculture and food sovereignty ministry, operates a sport-fishing census through which recreational sea anglers must file a comunicazione of their activity, and the ministry periodically renews or extends the validity of notifications already issued. The practical catch for visitors is how you log in — access to the census has run exclusively through Italian digital identity credentials (SPID, the electronic identity card, or the national services card) since 2022, which most short-term visitors do not hold, so this is worth resolving with a charter operator or the ministry before travelling rather than at the harbour. Freshwater is a separate world, licensed by region rather than nationally, and usually needing a local association permit for the specific water on top of the regional licence.
IT.seasons: Both Italian spots are freshwater and both are shaped more by water conditions than by dates. The Po in Emilia-Romagna fishes summer nights for wels catfish, a spring pre-spawn window, and comes good again once a flood recedes — that last point matters on a river that floods hard. Lake Garda is a spring lake trout fishery, turns to pike in autumn, and is best early in the morning before the wind gets up, which on Garda it reliably does. Closed seasons, permitted rod numbers and trolling rules differ by region and, on Garda, by shore — Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino each license their own side of the same lake.
IT.water: The two published Italian spots are both intermediate freshwater, and both are bigger than their reputations suggest. The Po is Italy's largest river and now one of Europe's serious wels catfish fisheries, also holding carp and zander, fished from banks and boats along a heavily modified channel. Lake Garda is an alpine-fed lake straddling three regions, holding lake trout, northern pike and whitefish, with an endemic carpione that is fully protected and must be returned. Garda's shape — deep, clear, windy, mountain-walled — makes it as much a weather fishery as a species one.
IT.sourceNotes: The MASAF comunicazione for recreational sea fishing, the sport-fishing census, and SPID/CIE/CNS-only access since 2 May 2022 verified against masaf.gov.it. Regional freshwater licensing and the three-region split on Garda come from the existing researched spot rows. NOT verified: what a visitor without Italian digital credentials should do instead, and the RecFishing daily catch-reporting app named in the countries.ts blurb — the app is not mentioned in this prose because it could not be confirmed on a ministry page this session.

authority.name: Norwegian Environment Agency — national fishing fee

links.name: Miljødirektoratet — pay the fishing fee
Norwegian Environment Agency — rules for recreational fishing in rivers and lakes

NO.regulations: Sea fishing in Norway needs no licence: the Environment Agency states plainly that no national fishing fee is required to use a rod or hand line in the sea. Rivers are different. To fish a river system holding salmon, sea trout or Arctic char you must pay the national fishing fee (fiskeravgift) for the season and carry proof of payment — and, because fishing rights belong to the landowner, you must also buy a licence or permit from them.
NO.licensing: Norway is the clearest split on this list: the sea is free and the salmon rivers are not. The Environment Agency confirms you do not need to pay the national fishing fee to fish with a rod or hand line in the sea, and you may fish there for salmon, sea trout and sea char from the shore year-round, subject to local bylaws. For rivers and lakes holding anadromous fish — salmon, sea trout, Arctic char — you must pay the national fishing fee before fishing during the ordinary season, always carry proof of payment, and produce it on request. Crucially, the fee is not permission to fish: fishing rights belong to the landowner, so you must buy a fishing licence or other permit from them as well. The fee itself goes to a state fund used to maintain those stocks. On rivers like the Alta, the landowner permit is the real bottleneck.
NO.seasons: Norwegian fishing is concentrated into short, intense windows at opposite ends of the year. The Alta salmon peaks in June and July and is fished through the night under the midnight sun, coming alive after a rise in water. Lofoten is the winter fishery: the skrei — migrating Arctic cod — arrive from January to April, which is the reason to be there, with midnight-sun summer fishing and slack tide over the banks as the secondary options. So Norway is genuinely a two-season destination, and the two seasons want different clothing, different tackle and different expectations. Gear brought from abroad must be disinfected before fishing salmon rivers, which is a biosecurity requirement to plan for rather than a formality.
NO.water: The two published Norwegian spots represent the country's two famous fisheries. The Alta in Finnmark is among the world's most storied Atlantic salmon rivers, and also among the hardest to get on: beats are allocated by lottery and largely reserved for locals, so access is very limited and advanced anglers plan years out. The Lofoten skrei grounds in Nordland are the opposite in accessibility — open saltwater for Atlantic cod, halibut and coalfish, fished from boats among the islands, needing no licence at all. One is a permit problem, the other is a weather problem.
NO.sourceNotes: The fee's application to salmon/sea trout/Arctic char river systems, the requirement to carry proof, the separate landowner permit, the fund's purpose, and no fee for rod or hand line in the sea all verified against environmentagency.no (Miljødirektoratet's English site). Age exemptions deliberately not stated: the agency page describes family fee categories and does not confirm the under-18 exemption a search summary suggested. Alta lottery allocation and gear disinfection come from the existing researched spot row.

authority.name: Svenska fiskeregler — recreational fishing rules (county boards and SwAM)

links.name: Havs- och vattenmyndigheten — Fiskekartan (fishing permit map)
Svenska fiskeregler — recreational fishing

SE.regulations: Sweden allows free rod fishing along the coast and on its five largest lakes — Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren and Storsjön — with the rules for those waters published jointly by the county administrative boards and the Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management. Everywhere else, fishing rights belong to someone: you buy a fiskekort from the local fishing conservation area, or ask the rights holder. Fiskekartan maps which is which.
SE.licensing: Sweden has the most generous access rules on this list, and the boundary is geographic rather than bureaucratic. Along the coast and on the five great lakes — Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren and Storsjön in Jämtland — recreational rod fishing is free, and the applicable rules are published on Svenska fiskeregler, the joint official site of the county administrative boards and the Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management. Outside those waters, fishing rights are private: most managed waters are organised into fishing conservation areas that sell a fiskekort granting permission, and where no such association exists you ask whoever holds the rights. The agency's Fiskekartan service maps the conservation areas, the species present and where permits are sold, which makes checking a specific water straightforward before you travel. Free does not mean unregulated — size rules and seasonal closures still apply.
SE.seasons: Sweden's season is a spring-and-autumn affair with a summer lull for predators. Vänern is trolled for salmon and lake trout from April to June and fishes pike in the bays in autumn, with overcast days preferred. The Stockholm archipelago runs the same shape — pike in April and May, then September to November, best when it is calm and grey. Mörrum, the salmon river, has a spring run from April to June and autumn sea trout in September and October, and responds to rain; its season dates, quotas and release rules are set annually rather than fixed, so last year's plan is not this year's rules. In some bays, seasonal closures protect spawning pike — a county-level rule worth checking.
SE.water: Three published Swedish spots, and they show how much variety the free-fishing rule opens up. Lake Vänern in Värmland is inland-sea trolling water for landlocked salmon, lake trout and northern pike. The River Mörrum in Blekinge is the opposite: a famous, tightly managed Atlantic salmon and sea trout river fished on booked beats, and the one Swedish spot where the permit matters most. The Stockholm archipelago is beginner-friendly brackish saltwater among thousands of islands for pike, perch and zander — free to fish with a rod, minutes from a capital city, which is close to unique in Europe.
SE.sourceNotes: Free coastal and five-great-lakes rod fishing, the naming of those five lakes, svenskafiskeregler.se as the county boards' and SwAM's joint official site, fishing conservation areas selling fiskekort, asking the rights holder otherwise, and Fiskekartan's coverage all verified against havochvatten.se and svenskafiskeregler.se. Mörrum's annually-set season and beat rules come from the existing researched spot row. Size limits deliberately omitted.

authority.name: Metsähallitus Eräluvat — fishing permits and the fisheries management fee

FI.regulations: Finland charges a state fisheries management fee, payable by anglers aged 18 to 69 who fish with lures or traps or catch crayfish. For single-rod fishing the fee alone is sufficient permission in many parts of the country. A separate permit from the water owner is additionally required for fishing with several rods or traps, for crayfishing, and in rapids, flowing waters and special sites — which covers most Metsähallitus fishing destinations.
FI.licensing: Finland's system is unusually well suited to visitors, provided you understand the two layers. The state fisheries management fee applies to anglers aged 18 to 69 fishing with lures or traps, or crayfishing, and where you are fishing with a single rod that fee is by itself sufficient permission across much of the country. The second layer is the water owner's permit, and Metsähallitus — the state land and water manager — is explicit that it becomes necessary when you fish with several rods or with traps, when crayfishing, and when fishing in rapids and flowing waters or at special sites, and that most of its own fishing destinations fall into that category. So the good rivers generally need both. Finland's everyman's-right tradition also leaves simple methods — ice fishing and basic float fishing — outside the fee regime, which is why a winter trip here has almost no paperwork.
FI.seasons: Finland has two seasons worth travelling for and they could not be less alike. The Tornio salmon run climbs from June to August and is fished through bright midnight-sun nights, best after a rise in water; its season dates and quotas are agreed jointly between Finland and Sweden and change from year to year, so they must be checked annually rather than assumed. Lake Saimaa runs a conventional open-water calendar — zander at dusk through summer, pike in autumn — and then becomes an ice fishery in February and March, which is genuinely one of the better beginner introductions to fishing anywhere. Seasonal boat and net restrictions on Saimaa protect the endangered Saimaa ringed seal.
FI.water: Both published Finnish spots sit at the accessible end for their type. The Tornio in Lapland is a large, wild border river for Atlantic salmon, grayling and whitefish, and it is advanced water — big flows, long casts, short season. Lake Saimaa in South Savo is the opposite: Europe's fourth-largest lake system, a beginner-friendly maze of islands and channels holding northern pike, zander and perch, fishable from a boat in summer and from the ice in late winter. Gear disinfection is required on the salmon river to guard against Gyrodactylus salaris, a parasite that has devastated salmon stocks elsewhere in the region.
FI.sourceNotes: The fisheries management fee's 18-69 age range, its application to lure/trap fishing and crayfishing, single-rod sufficiency in many areas, and the specific circumstances requiring a water owner's permit (several rods, traps, crayfishing, rapids and flowing waters, special sites, most Metsähallitus sites) verified against eraluvat.fi. The transitional exemption for those aged 65+ as of 31 December 2023 that appears on that page is deliberately omitted as a dated rule likely to go stale. Tornio's bilateral season-setting and the Saimaa seal restrictions come from the existing researched spot rows.

links.name: DFFE — forms and permits
DFFE — recreational fishing permit guideline

ZA.regulations: Marine recreational fishing in South Africa requires a permit from the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment. These can now be bought through the department's online platform — register, choose the permit type and validity, pay and download it — or still over the counter at a South African Post Office branch for anyone without internet access. The Marine Living Resources Fund issues them. Freshwater licensing is provincial instead.
ZA.licensing: South Africa requires a recreational permit for marine fishing, issued under the Marine Living Resources Fund by the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment. Until recently the Post Office counter was the only realistic route; the department now runs an online platform where you register, select the permit type and the period of validity, pay and download the permit immediately, with Post Office branches retained for people without internet access. That change matters for visitors, because it means the permit can be arranged before arrival rather than during. Permit type depends on what you intend to do — shore angling, boat angling and other categories are separate — so pick deliberately. Freshwater fishing is licensed provincially and separately. Marine protected areas add a second layer of rules that a permit does not override.
ZA.seasons: South African fishing splits along the two coasts and their very different water. In False Bay, yellowtail run from November to April, tuna are available year-round when the weather settles, and the practical rule is to be out early before the southeaster gets up — Cape fishing is dictated by wind more than by season. On the KwaZulu-Natal coast, Sodwana's couta season runs April to September, with gamefish through summer and calm mornings the window. Between them the two spots cover most of the year, which is unusual, but neither is weather-independent: the Cape in particular loses days to wind at any time of year.
ZA.water: Both published South African spots are saltwater and both sit inside protected areas, which shapes the fishing as much as the species do. Cape Point and False Bay is advanced, cold, Atlantic-influenced water for yellowtail, snoek and yellowfin tuna, with large parts of the bay and the Table Mountain marine protected area closed to taking anything. Sodwana Bay in KwaZulu-Natal is warm Indian Ocean water for king mackerel, giant trevally and sailfish, inside the iSimangaliso World Heritage Site, where launch sites and no-take zones are tightly controlled and launching is part of the experience. In both places, knowing the zone boundaries is as important as holding the permit.
ZA.sourceNotes: The DFFE online recreational permit platform (register, choose type and validity, pay, download), the Marine Living Resources Fund as issuer, and retained South African Post Office counter sales for those without internet access verified against dffe.gov.za and fishing.dffe.gov.za. Provincial freshwater licensing stated in general terms only. MPA and iSimangaliso zoning come from the existing researched spot rows.

authority.name: Santa Cruz — SIPESQ sport fishing permits

links.name: Tierra del Fuego — Ministerio de Producción y Ambiente, pesca deportiva
Reglamento General de Pesca Deportiva Continental Patagónica

AR.regulations: Argentine fishing licences are provincial. Santa Cruz issues permits through its SIPESQ system and Tierra del Fuego through its own digital permit system, and in both the permit is personal, compulsory and non-transferable. Season dates are set provincially each year — Santa Cruz has run an October-to-September licence year, Tierra del Fuego a November-to-May season — and Patagonian fishing also falls under the general continental Patagonian sport fishing regulation.
AR.licensing: Argentina has no national recreational licence; the province issues it, and in Patagonia the province also sets the season. Santa Cruz sells permits through SIPESQ, its online system, and Tierra del Fuego through its own digital permit platform, which also handles access reservations for the sectors it controls. In both provinces the permit is explicitly personal, compulsory and non-transferable, so each angler needs their own and it cannot be shared or passed on. Above the provincial rules sits the Reglamento General de Pesca Deportiva Continental Patagónica, the general regulation for continental Patagonian sport fishing. The other half of Argentine access is not regulatory at all: several of the best fisheries have no public road frontage and are fished exclusively through licensed lodges booked well in advance, so the permit is rarely the hard part of the trip to arrange.
AR.seasons: Patagonian trout fishing is a southern-summer season, and the dates are provincial rather than national. Santa Cruz has run a licence year from October to the following September, while Tierra del Fuego's season has opened on 1 November and closed at the start of May. On the ground that means Jurassic Lake fishes across the provincial season with calm mornings and overcast days best, and the Río Grande's sea trout peak from January to March, fished in the evening and at night when the wind eases. Further north on the Paraná, golden dorado run from September to April and fish best in low, clear water early in the morning. Season dates are re-set each year, so confirm them with the province before booking anything.
AR.water: Argentina gives AnglerDeck two world-famous fisheries and one that deserves to be. Jurassic Lake — Lago Strobel in Santa Cruz — is a landlocked lake producing rainbow trout of a size that has no real parallel, fished on foot, and reachable only through private lodges: there are no public roads and no facilities. The Río Grande in Tierra del Fuego is the sea-run brown trout river, similarly lodge-based. The Paraná at Paso de la Patria in Corrientes is the contrast: warm, huge, subtropical river water for golden dorado, surubí and pacú, fished from boats with guides. Catch-and-release with barbless hooks is enforced on both Patagonian fisheries.
AR.sourceNotes: Provincial permit systems (SIPESQ for Santa Cruz, the Tierra del Fuego digital permit system with sector reservations), the permit being personal, compulsory and non-transferable, the 2025/26 Santa Cruz licence year of 1 October to 30 September, the Tierra del Fuego season of 1 November to early May, and the existence of the Reglamento General de Pesca Deportiva Continental Patagónica verified against santacruz.gob.ar, tierradelfuego.gob.ar and argentina.gob.ar. Season dates are described as provincially re-set each year rather than as fixed, because they are. The one-fish and mandatory-release specifics published for the 2025/26 Tierra del Fuego season are deliberately omitted under rule 3.

authority.name: Governo Federal — solicitar licença de pescador amador

links.name: Ministério da Pesca e Aquicultura — amateur and sport fisher registration
IEF Minas Gerais — piracema

BR.regulations: Brazil issues a single federal amateur fishing licence, applied for online, valid for one year across the whole national territory, in separate shore and vessel categories. Applicants receive a provisional licence while the definitive one is issued. The piracema spawning closure then restricts or bans fishing over the southern summer — states publish their own dates, and Mato Grosso do Sul and others have run it from 1 November to 28 February.
BR.licensing: Brazil is the simplest licensing country on this list: one federal amateur fishing licence, applied for electronically, valid for a year throughout the national territory. It is issued in two categories — shore-based and vessel-based — so choose to match how you will actually fish, and everyone including fee-exempt applicants receives a provisional licence valid while the definitive document is produced. Older Brazilian applicants are exempt from the fee under long-standing law. Because the licence is national, the complexity in Brazil is not the permit but everything layered on top of it: states set their own additional restrictions, some species are protected in some states and not others, and access to indigenous territories requires separate permission entirely, which is why the remote fisheries are fished through licensed operators. Confirm the state rules alongside the federal licence.
BR.seasons: Brazilian fishing is organised around water level and the spawning closure. Both spots we publish are dry-season fisheries: the Pantanal fishes best from June to October when water drops and clears, and the Rio Negro from September to March when the lagoons fall and topwater fishing comes into its own at first light. The reason the calendar looks like that is the piracema — the spawning migration — during which fishing is banned or heavily restricted. State environment agencies publish the dates and they have commonly run from 1 November to the end of February, but they are set per state and per basin rather than nationally, so the closure that applies to your trip is the state's. Fishing during it also carries licence-suspension consequences.
BR.water: The two published Brazilian spots are both freshwater and both are properly remote. The Pantanal in Mato Grosso do Sul is the world's largest tropical wetland — a seasonal floodplain fished for golden dorado, pacú and pintado catfish as the water falls. The Rio Negro in Amazonas is blackwater river and lagoon fishing for peacock bass, with arowana and piranha alongside, and it is advanced water reached by liveaboard or lodge rather than by road. Both reward going in the dry season and both are fished with guides, which is as much about navigation and permissions as it is about finding fish.
BR.sourceNotes: The federal licence — electronic application, one-year validity across national territory, separate shore (desembarcada) and vessel (embarcada) categories, provisional licence pending the definitive one, and statutory fee exemption for older applicants — verified against gov.br federal service pages. Piracema dates verified against state environment agency pages (IMASUL Mato Grosso do Sul, IEF Minas Gerais, SEMA Mato Grosso), which is why they are attributed to states rather than stated as a national rule. Fee amounts and the federal weight quota in the existing spot row are deliberately omitted.

links.name: CONAPESCA-01-016 — sport and recreational fishing permit

MX.regulations: Mexico issues sport fishing permits through CONAPESCA, the national aquaculture and fisheries commission, to Mexican nationals and foreign visitors alike. Permits are individual, non-extendable and non-transferable, and come in one-day, one-week, one-month and annual forms. Fishing from a vessel or underwater requires a permit, and vessel-based fishing additionally requires the permits set out in the federal duties law. Buy before you board.
MX.licensing: Mexican sport fishing permits come from CONAPESCA, the national aquaculture and fisheries commission, and the rules are refreshingly explicit: permits are issued to natural persons whether Mexican or foreign, and each is individual, non-extendable and non-transferable. You can buy them for a day, a week, a month or a year, which suits everything from an afternoon panga trip to a season. A permit is required to fish recreationally from a vessel or underwater, and fishing aboard a vessel also brings in the permits required under the federal duties law — so on a charter, confirm what the operator holds and what you are expected to hold yourself before leaving the dock, since the permit is personal to you rather than to the boat. Marine protected areas and national parks impose separate access rules that a CONAPESCA permit does not satisfy on its own.
MX.seasons: Mexico's Pacific and Caribbean coasts run different calendars, and all three published spots are coastal. On the Baja side, Cabo San Lucas fishes striped marlin from October through June, with tuna and dorado in summer and early mornings best; La Paz and Espíritu Santo turn on roosterfish from May to October, hunted along the beaches at dawn. On the Caribbean side, Ascension Bay holds permit year-round — one of the few places that can be said of — with tarpon from March to September, and bright calm mornings the ideal. That spread means Mexico is close to a year-round destination, provided you move between coasts rather than expecting one to deliver everything.
MX.water: All three Mexican spots are saltwater, and they divide into flats and blue water. Ascension Bay in Quintana Roo is advanced flats fishing for bonefish, permit and tarpon inside the Sian Ka'an biosphere reserve, where fishing runs catch-and-release through licensed guides and independent access is restricted. Cabo San Lucas is intermediate offshore fishing for striped marlin, dorado and yellowfin tuna where the Pacific meets the Sea of Cortez. La Paz and Espíritu Santo is advanced inshore and island water for roosterfish, dorado and yellowtail, inside a national park with protected zones. Roosterfish are a release fishery in Mexico, which is worth knowing before booking a trip built around them.
MX.sourceNotes: CONAPESCA permits being issued to nationals and foreigners, individual, non-extendable and non-transferable, available as day/week/month/year, required for vessel-based and underwater recreational fishing, and vessel fishing requiring the permits under the Ley Federal de Derechos, all verified against gob.mx CONAPESCA pages. NOT verified and therefore not claimed: that shore fishing needs no permit, and that every person aboard needs one whether they fish or not — both appear in the countries.ts blurb and the existing spot rows. The billfish daily limit in an existing spot row is omitted under rule 3.

authority.name: Japan Fisheries Agency — recreational fishing by foreign nationals

links.name: Japan Fisheries Agency — inland water recreational fishing system
Japan Fisheries Agency — basic rules for recreational and coastal fishing

JP.regulations: Japan treats recreational fishing as minor capture rather than licensed fishing. Foreign nationals may fish from shore with rod, hand line, net or spear, and from vessels under three tons; fishing from vessels of three tons or more is restricted to Japanese vessels operated by Japanese fishers. Inland waters work differently: fisheries cooperatives set governor-approved rules with fees, permits (yugyoken) and defined seasons. Prefectural rules apply throughout — check locally first.
JP.licensing: Japan has no recreational fishing licence in the European sense, but it does have rules that catch visitors out. The Fisheries Agency treats recreational fishing as 'minor capture', and for foreign nationals sets out what is permitted by method and by vessel: from shore, rod, hand line, net and spear fishing are allowed; from vessels under three tons, similar gear plus trolling in designated areas and seasons; from vessels of three tons or more, the activity is restricted to Japanese vessels operated by Japanese fishers. Inland waters are governed separately and locally. Inland fisheries cooperatives set yugyo rules approved by the prefectural governor, and those rules fix the fee, the permit — the yugyoken — and the fishing period for the water they manage. Prefectural fishery adjustment regulations sit above both, and the Agency's advice is to confirm the rules for the specific region in advance.
JP.seasons: Japanese fishing is tightly seasonal and the seasons are set locally rather than nationally. At Nikkō, Lake Yunoko fishes from spring into autumn — roughly April to September on the cooperative's calendar — with the evening rise the reliable window and autumn worth it for the colour as much as the fish. Tokyo Bay runs a different year: summer nights, an autumn run from September to November, and fishing the tide around the bridge lights. Because inland seasons are defined by each cooperative's governor-approved rules rather than by a national date, the season for the specific water is the one that matters, and it is set out in the same document as the permit and the fee.
JP.water: The two published Japanese spots could hardly be less alike, which is a fair picture of the country. Lake Yunoko at Nikkō, in Tochigi, is a small mountain lake inside a national park, beginner-friendly fly water for brook, rainbow and brown trout, and strictly catch-and-release: fish may not be removed from the lake. Tokyo Bay is intermediate urban saltwater in the middle of the world's largest metropolitan area, for Japanese sea bass, yellowtail amberjack and flathead, fished at night around structure and lights. Some ports and harbour areas prohibit angling outright, so posted signs matter more here than almost anywhere else on the site.
JP.sourceNotes: Permitted methods for foreign nationals by vessel size (shore; under three tons; three tons or more restricted to Japanese vessels and fishers), trolling in ministerially designated areas and seasons, and the instruction to confirm regional rules in advance, verified against the Japan Fisheries Agency page on recreational fishing by foreign nationals. The inland cooperative system — governor-approved yugyo rules fixing fee, yugyoken permit and fishing period — verified against the Agency's inland waters page. The Agency's English-language site does not cover recreational fishing, so both sources are Japanese-language official pages.

authority.name: Federal Agency for Fishery (Rosrybolovstvo) — amateur and sport fishing

links.name: Rosrybolovstvo — fishing rules for the Northern fishery basin

RU.regulations: Russia has no general recreational fishing licence: amateur fishing on public waters is free, subject to the fishing rules for the relevant fishery basin. On designated fishing grounds and sites, however, fishing requires a putyovka — a document confirming a paid service contract, which states the permitted catch, the area, the methods and the validity period. The named salmon and trout rivers are managed this way, through licensed camps.
RU.licensing: There is no recreational fishing licence in Russia, and for ordinary fishing there is nothing to buy: the Federal Agency for Fishery states that citizens may fish public waters freely and free of charge, in accordance with the fishing rules for the relevant fishery basin — those rules are published per basin and are where the real restrictions live. The exception is the one that matters for every Russian fishery on this site. On designated fishing grounds and sites, amateur fishing is conducted under a putyovka, a document confirming a paid services contract that specifies the volume of catch agreed, the area within the site, the permitted methods and the period of validity. The famous salmon and trout rivers operate on exactly that basis, through licensed camps, so access is arranged commercially and well in advance rather than bought on arrival.
RU.seasons: Both Russian fisheries are brief far-northern or far-eastern seasons. On the Kola Peninsula, the Atlantic salmon run peaks in June and July, fished under the midnight sun and best after a rise in water. Kamchatka's rainbow trout season runs July to September, with mouse-pattern fishing in late summer its signature, and Pacific salmon runs starting in June. Neither is a destination you can improvise: the season is short, the camps allocate rods in advance, and the paperwork is part of the booking. Protected-area and border-zone restrictions in these regions can require documentation arranged ahead of travel, so treat the permit timeline as part of the season planning.
RU.water: The two published Russian spots are both advanced fly fisheries at the remote end of the site. The Kola Peninsula rivers in Murmansk Oblast are among the strongest Atlantic salmon rivers in the world, also holding brown trout and Arctic char, and run almost entirely through licensed camps. Kamchatka's rivers hold wild rainbow trout, king salmon and char in a volcanic landscape with effectively no road access, reached by helicopter and fished from camps or rafts. In both places the fishing is not the logistical problem — getting there, and being permitted to be there, is.
RU.sourceNotes: Free amateur fishing on public waters subject to basin fishing rules, and the putyovka requirement on designated fishing grounds and sites (specifying agreed catch volume, area, methods and validity), verified against fish.gov.ru. NOT verified this session: the specific border-zone permit requirements near the Norwegian and Finnish frontiers claimed in the existing Kola spot row — the prose says only that such restrictions can require documentation arranged in advance, which the camps handle. Fishing rules are basin-specific and were not read per basin.

links.name: gov.pl — issue of a fishing card (karta wędkarska)

PL.regulations: Poland requires two things of an angler. The document authorising amateur fishing is the karta wędkarska, the fishing card, issued by the district (powiat) authority. On top of that you need a permit — a zezwolenie — for the specific fishing ground from whoever holds the fishing rights there; for waters managed by Wody Polskie these are bought online, and from January 2026 exclusively so. Check both before fishing.
PL.licensing: Polish fishing needs a document and a permit, and they come from different places. The document authorising amateur fishing is the karta wędkarska, issued by the powiat (district) authority, and the second requirement is a permit for the particular water from the entity holding the fishing rights in that fishing district. For the many fishing grounds managed by Wody Polskie, the state water authority, those permits are sold through its online system as annual or periodic e-permits: you select the location and permit type and pay online, and the PDF with its QR code is the document you carry — no printing required. From January 2026 that route is electronic only. Where a water is managed by an angling association instead, the permit comes from them. Plan for both steps rather than assuming one covers the other.
PL.seasons: Polish fishing follows a conventional Central European calendar built around predator closed seasons. On the Vistula, zander fish best at dusk, asp come on in summer, and autumn brings a general feeding window. The Masurian lakes peak for pike from September to November, fish zander at dusk, and then turn into an ice fishery in January and February. Zander and pike both carry closed seasons and minimum sizes under Polish rules — the closures are the thing to check before booking a spring trip, since they fall in the spawning period and are what determine whether a predator trip is possible at all. The permit for the water will normally set out the rules that apply to it.
PL.water: Both published Polish spots are freshwater and they represent the two halves of Polish fishing. The Vistula in Mazovia is the country's great river — a large, braided, sandy-bedded channel holding zander, wels catfish and asp, and intermediate water where reading the river matters. The Masurian Lake District in Warmia-Masuria is the opposite: a beginner-friendly maze of connected lakes for northern pike, zander and perch, one of the largest lake districts in Europe, fishable from a boat in summer and from the ice in winter. Between them they are a good argument for Poland as an underrated fishing destination.
PL.sourceNotes: The karta wędkarska as the authorising document, and the separate zezwolenie for the specific fishing district, verified against gov.pl and samorzad.gov.pl. The Wody Polskie e-permit process — annual or periodic, online purchase, QR-coded PDF, electronic-only from 1 January 2026 — verified against the Wody Polskie page. NOT VERIFIED, and deliberately absent from this prose: the claim in the countries.ts blurb and in both Polish spot rows that foreign visitors are exempt from the karta wędkarska requirement. Three official routes were tried — the ISAP statute PDF (CAPTCHA), the eli.gov.pl copy (unreadable binary) and a powiat information page (exemptions only in an unfetched PDF). The exemption is plausibly Article 7 of the Ustawa o rybactwie śródlądowym, but until it is read on an official page it must not be published.
